messages.author: bfa43814f6ba1969
messages.subject: Re: Basic Question
parts:
Hi,

The predict function calculates factor scores based on the fitted model and the observed data. The equation for regression factor scores is the inverse of the indicator covariance matrix multiplied by the vector of estimated covariances between the indicators and the factor. This is quite different from the equations that you provide below. 

Mikko

Hi,

Can you provide the R code that you are using to do the calculations?

This code demonstrates that the scores are regression factor scores and calculated as discussed in this thread:

## The industrialization and Political Democracy Example 
## Bollen (1989), page 332
model <- ' 
# latent variable definitions
ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3

dem60 =~ y1 + a*y2 + b*y3 + c*y4
dem65 =~ y5 + a*y6 + b*y7 + c*y8

# regressions
dem60 ~ ind60
dem65 ~ ind60 + dem60

# residual correlations
y1 ~~ y5
y2 ~~ y4 + y6
y3 ~~ y7
y4 ~~ y8
y6 ~~ y8
'

fit <- sem(model, data=PoliticalDemocracy)

f1 <- predict(fit)[,1]

# Calculate the same manually
ca <- inspect(fit,"cov.all")
n <- colnames(PoliticalDemocracy)
f2 <- as.matrix(PoliticalDemocracy) %*% solve(ca[n,n],ca[n,"ind60"])  
f2 <- f2 - mean(f2)

cbind(f1,f2)


Mikko

Hi

Regression factor scores are calculated based on all indicators, and not just the indicators of one factor. If you compare my example with yours, you can see that I did not subset the indicator covariance matrix like you do. That should explain the different results.

But let’s take a step back: What is it that you really want to do? Do you want to calculate factor scores or do you want to calculate some kind of model-based predictions. These are two different things. If you want to predict, what exactly are you predicting and with what?

Mikko

On 09 May 2016, at 15:27 , rishabh sharma <risha...@gmail.com> wrote:


Okay...I've got a question on using mat.regress for getting the regression equations.

Just to be clear, that is just a packaged version of inverting the independent variables covariance matrix and multiplying it with the vector of covariance between the independent and dependent variables.
We know that SEM uses a set of equations (measurement model and structural model) to predict Y.
I do not think that you should think of SEM in terms of prediction, but in terms of explanation. You are trying to explain the relationships between the observed variables with the model.

For instance, below are the theoretical equations used in the model:

# measurement model
ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3.....(1)
dem60 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4.....(2)
dem65 =~ y5 + y6 + y7 + y8....(3)
# structural model
dem60 ~ ind60.....(4)
dem65 ~ ind60 + dem60....(5)

To get the regression scores for each equation, I will be entering the covariance matrix for each of them and getting the beta coefficients.Is this the right way to go?
Note that these are not five regression equations, but a lot more. A factor such as
ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3

means that the factor explains all three indicators, so each indicator has an equation. You do not use the SEM equations to calculate factor scores.

Mikko

On 10 May 2016, at 10:16 , rishabh sharma <risha...@gmail.com> wrote:


Yep, I do understand that the mat.regress function is simply performing the matrix multiplication. However, I want to discuss your second point in detail. As I have indicated above that I do want to know the relationships between the observed variables.But I would also like to benchmark my prediction accuracy with the results of the logistic regression and decision trees. The bone of contention here is that my client is unsure of using a new technique like SEM and wants to categorically, compare the prediction accuracy with other 'more established' techniques. Hope you understand my predicament here…J

Now, coming back to the point if it is possible to predict output using SEM. I do agree that SEM is not just a set of regression equations but alot more. Furthermore, I have my doubts that if we are calculating the regression scores using five different covariance matrices and five mathematical equations, we are considering them to be effectively independent of each other (which is not the case).

I guess the answer then is no: You cannot take the SEM equations and calculate predictions of Ys because the Ys are expressed as functions of latent variables and you cannot predict based on something that you cannot observe. 

What you can do is to calculate factor scores, and then calculate predictions based on the scores using the SEM equations. The problem with this approach is that the factor scores are calculated based on all indicators, including the one that you want to predict. If your prediction equations require data on the variable being predicted, then prediction would be quite pointless, right? 

If you want to do linear predictions using the information from the SEM model, you can use the model implied covariance matrix to calculate the prediction equations.
To conclude, even I believe that mat.regress is not the best way to calculate the regression scores in SEM. Is there some other way I can predict Y's using SEM?

The best way to calculate regression factor scores would be to use lavaan’s predict function. You can do that with matrix algebra (solve and %*%) or with mat.regress as well. 

Mikko

PS: Apologies for my stubbornness but predicting Y's using the SEM results is of prime importance here. Also, I really appreciate the time you have given till now in trying to solve the above problem.

parts: I guess the answer then is no: You cannot take the SEM equations and calculate predictions of Ys because the Ys are expressed as functions of latent variables and you cannot predict based on something that you cannot observe.
Although, I do agree that we cannot measure the latent variables but they can be predicted by multiplying the factor scores and the observed predictor variables i.e X's.

What you can do is to calculate factor scores, and then calculate predictions based on the scores using the SEM equations. The problem with this approach is that the factor scores are calculated based on all indicators, including the one that you want to predict. If your prediction equations require data on the variable being predicted, then prediction would be quite pointless, right?

I am not sure what you mean by this. We are taking the factor scores (by using the covariance matrix) from the training data and applying it to the test data.I am talking about predicting the latent variables by multiplying the factor scores and observed predictor variables. Then, we can predict the Ys from the latent variables. Isn't it a similar process to what we do in regression.i.e get scores from the training data and using the scores to predict the out of sample data.
The best way to calculate regression factor scores would be to use lavaan’s predict function. You can do that with matrix algebra (solve and %*%) or with mat.regress as well.

Yes, I am going to use lavpredict function to predict the output now. However, I have one more question to ask. If i predicted Y by using a sequential set of equations as indicated below:

ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3.....(1)
dem60 ~ ind60.....(2)
dem65 ~ ind60 + dem60....(3) 
dem60 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4.....(4)
dem65 =~ y5 + y6 + y7 + y8....(5)

such that I predicted ind60 using mat.regress function from x1,x2 and x3. Then, I used the model implied variance to calculate the outputs for (2) and (3). Finally, I used the output of (2),(3) to predict Y's. Will this be correct?

On 12 May 2016, at 13:03 , rishabh sharma <risha...@gmail.com> wrote:


I guess the answer then is no: You cannot take the SEM equations and calculate predictions of Ys because the Ys are expressed as functions of latent variables and you cannot predict based on something that you cannot observe. 

Although, I do agree that we cannot measure the latent variables but they can be predicted by multiplying the factor scores and the observed predictor variables i.e X's.

What you can do is to calculate factor scores, and then calculate predictions based on the scores using the SEM equations. The problem with this approach is that the factor scores are calculated based on all indicators, including the one that you want to predict. If your prediction equations require data on the variable being predicted, then prediction would be quite pointless, right? 

I am not sure what you mean by this. We are taking the factor scores (by using the covariance matrix) from the training data and applying it to the test data.I am talking about predicting the latent variables by multiplying the factor scores and observed predictor variables. Then, we can predict the Ys from the latent variables. Isn't it a similar process to what we do in regression.i.e get scores from the training data and using the scores to predict the out of sample data.

You can do that, but it would be pretty pointless. Consider for example predicting x1 based on regression factor scores. Because factor scores are calculated based on all indicators, you need x1 to calculate scores for any of the factors. This means that the prediction equation for x1 will contain x1 itself as one of the terms. That is like requiring that you must know what the what the weather is going to be like tomorrow to forecast tomorrow’s weather.

The best way to calculate regression factor scores would be to use lavaan’s predict function. You can do that with matrix algebra (solve and %*%) or with mat.regress as well. 

Yes, I am going to use lavpredict function to predict the output now. However, I have one more question to ask. If i predicted Y by using a sequential set of equations as indicated below:

ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3.....(1)
dem60 ~ ind60.....(2)
dem65 ~ ind60 + dem60....(3) 
dem60 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4.....(4)
dem65 =~ y5 + y6 + y7 + y8....(5)

such that I predicted ind60 using mat.regress function from x1,x2 and x3. Then, I used the model implied variance to calculate the outputs for (2) and (3). Finally, I used the output of (2),(3) to predict Y's. Will this be correct?

You can calculate predictions in many different ways and I do not think that one is more correct than another. Depends on which indicators you use, what you predict, and how you want to take the information from the estimated model into account. I would calculate the prediction equations with regression estimates based on the model implied matrix.

Mikko
